bib.title: AI Systems Performance Engineering, Chapter 5. GPU-Based Storage I/O Optimizations

question: How should storage and input pipelines be tuned so GPUs are never starved of data during large-scale training?
contributions: Storage layout, NVMe and filesystem tuning, GPUDirect Storage, DeepSeek 3FS, distributed filesystems and object stores, data loader and DALI/NeMo Curator tuning, a continuous profiling workflow

limits: Training-centred; inference weight loading is not discussed.
gdsio benchmark gives no GPU, SSD, filesystem or repeat count; numbers are round and look illustrative.
The 3FS vs Ceph comparison is quoted without a Ceph source or a hardware match.
GDS support lists are 'as of this writing' and will date.
practices: Pack small files into large shards (Arrow, TFRecord, Parquet, WebDataset) and read in about 1 MB chunks rather than 4 KB (Sequential Versus Random Read Patterns).
Use a none or mq-deadline scheduler on NVMe and raise read_ahead_kb from 128 KB to a few MB for streaming (Tuning NVMe).
Use multiple DataLoader workers with pin_memory=True, non_blocking=True, persistent_workers=True and a tuned prefetch_factor (default 2).
Use GDS with O_DIRECT and cuFile where the CPU is the copy bottleneck; it does not remove CPU orchestration.
A FUSE filesystem cannot provide a GDS path (GDS callout).
Keep NFS to a few nodes; use rsize/wsize 1 MiB, noatime; prefer parallel filesystems and stripe across OSTs for larger clusters.
Stage object-store data on local NVMe with parallel tools such as s5cmd, or use multithreaded range GETs.
Preprocess data offline (NeMo Curator) rather than training on raw text.
Scale data-loader workers and I/O bandwidth with GPU count.
Measure with num_workers=0 and CUDA events to separate Python cost from host-to-device copy cost; use nsys --trace=gds.
Change one or two things at a time and remeasure; keep a continuous profiling workflow.
Vary batch size with fixed all-reduce volume to tell communication-bound from compute-bound.
